planting.note: Set one-year-old crowns 6-8 inches deep in a trench in early spring once soil is workable, covering gradually as spears emerge over the season.

directions: Atlas was among the earlier Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids released before the later Jersey series, bred by crossing selected male parents to eliminate female seed-bearing plants and the volunteer seedling weediness they cause in a bed. Because no energy is spent on berry and seed production, Atlas channels more resources into spear number and thickness than open-pollinated heirlooms, and it carries improved tolerance to Fusarium crown rot compared to older strains. Skip harvest entirely the first year and take only a light cutting the second spring, letting the ferny top growth run all summer to recharge the crown. Established beds can remain productive for well over a decade with an annual fall topdressing of compost.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant dormant one-year crowns in a deep furrow in early spring, filling in soil in stages as new spears push through.

directions: Apollo is one of the original Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus releases, developed alongside Atlas and Eros before the breeding program's later Jersey-series introductions. Its all-male genetics mean plants never set the small red berries typical of female asparagus, so beds stay cleaner and free of the crowded volunteer seedlings that reduce spear size over time. Apollo produces a heavy early flush of medium-thick spears and shows good resistance to rust in humid regions. Wait until the third spring after crown planting to begin a full harvest season, cutting spears at soil level every one to two days during the peak flush.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Set crowns into a 6-8 inch deep trench as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, backfilling progressively through the season.

directions: Eros rounds out the trio of early Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids bred from crosses with the 'Rutgers Beacon' and related male lines, predating the better-known Jersey series. Like its siblings Atlas and Apollo, it directs all of its energy into spear production rather than seed set, giving heavier early yields than older open-pollinated Mary Washington-type strains. Give the crowns two full seasons to build a root system before any harvest, then cut spears daily during the flush to keep the plant signaling new growth. A well-maintained Eros bed rewards gardeners with a productive asparagus patch for fifteen years or more.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant one-year crowns in a trench in early spring in the northern half of its range, timing planting to local frost so young spears are not caught by a hard late freeze.

directions: Viking KB3 is an open-pollinated strain developed in Canada and long favored in short-season, cold-winter growing regions for its exceptional hardiness and reliable rust tolerance. Unlike the all-male Rutgers hybrids, Viking KB3 produces both male and female plants, so expect some volunteer seedlings to appear around the bed over time and thin them out to avoid overcrowding. Its spears are medium-thick with tight, purple-tinged tips and hold up well to the freeze-thaw cycles of prairie and northern climates. Because it is open-pollinated, saved seed from a healthy stand will grow true enough for home use, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sustaining asparagus patch.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

planting.note: In mild-winter regions, plant crowns in late winter to early spring in a deep, well-drained trench; in colder zones wait until the soil has warmed and danger of hard freeze has passed.

directions: California 500 is a widely grown open-pollinated selection developed for the mild-winter, low-chill growing conditions of California's commercial asparagus districts, where it has long served as a dependable field standard. It produces vigorous, uniform, medium-green spears with good tip retention over an extended cutting season in regions too warm for northern selections to go fully dormant. Because plants are not all-male, expect a mix of male and female asparagus and remove any weak or overly seedy female plants over the years to keep the stand productive. It performs best where winters are too mild for deep dormancy but summers still bring enough heat to fuel strong fern growth after the harvest window closes.
sources: California Department of Food and Agriculture

common_name: Waltham Washington Asparagus (Rust-Resistant Mary Washington Strain)

planting.note: Set crowns 6-8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring, backfilling as spears grow; direct seeding indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost is also an option for this open-pollinated strain.

directions: Waltham Washington was selected at the University of Massachusetts's Waltham Field Station from Mary Washington lines for improved cold hardiness and stronger resistance to asparagus rust, making it a reliable choice for shorter, colder growing seasons than the original Mary Washington tolerates well. Spears emerge thick and green with a light purple blush at the tightly closed tip, in the classic heirloom shape home gardeners expect. As an open-pollinated strain it produces both sexes, so female plants will drop red berries in late summer that can self-sow into the row if not managed. Allow two full seasons of unharvested fern growth before cutting begins, then harvest for six to eight weeks each spring once the bed is mature.

planting.note: Plant one-year crowns into a deep trench in early spring, covering gradually as spears develop through the growing season.

directions: Backlim comes from the same Dutch breeding program that produced Gijnlim, part of a family of hybrids bred in the Netherlands for uniform, high-yielding green asparagus grown both for fresh market and for forced early production under tunnels. It sends up thick, straight, deep-green spears with dense, tightly closed tips that hold their quality well during the flush of a heavy spring harvest. Like other modern Dutch hybrids, Backlim shows good vigor and reasonably even emergence, which simplifies daily cutting on a productive bed. Give the crowns at least two seasons to establish before harvesting, and maintain full fern growth after cutting ends each year to recharge the root system for the following spring.

planting.note: Set crowns in a deep, well-drained trench in early spring, filling in soil gradually as new spears emerge over the season.

directions: Larac is a French-bred green asparagus hybrid developed from INRA breeding lines and widely grown across French production regions for its reliable early emergence and consistent spear quality. Spears are medium to thick, cylindrical, and hold their tight tips well even during a fast spring flush, making the variety popular where harvest timing matters for fresh-market bunching. It shows solid tolerance to common rust and performs reliably across a range of soil types provided drainage is good. As with other named hybrids, resist harvesting until the crowns have had two full seasons to establish, then cut spears daily at ground level through the six-to-eight-week spring season.
sources: Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (INRA)

planting.note: Set dormant crowns or divisions in early spring while still leafless, burying the crown bud just at or slightly below soil level in rich, well-drained ground.

directions: Ruby is an older English-raised rhubarb selection valued for stalks that stay a rich wine-red well up their length rather than fading to green partway, giving a more visually striking harvest than many all-purpose varieties. Flavor is bright and tart with the moderate acidity typical of good culinary rhubarb, making it well suited to pies, sauces, and preserves where color matters as much as taste. Divide crowns every four to six years once the center of the clump begins to thin, replanting divisions with at least one strong bud each. Skip harvest the first year after planting and take only a light cutting the second spring to let the crown build reserves for a long productive life.

planting.note: Plant crowns or root divisions in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, setting the bud just below the soil surface.

directions: Colorado Red is a widely sold American heirloom selection prized for thick, deeply pigmented red stalks and the vigorous, cold-hardy habit that made it a staple in high-plains and mountain-region kitchen gardens. It tends to produce especially large, robust plants once established, with broad crinkled leaves shading a productive clump of stalks each spring. As with all rhubarb, only the stalks are eaten — the leaves contain concentrated oxalic acid and should always be removed and composted rather than consumed. Harvest by pulling stalks with a twisting motion rather than cutting, and stop picking by midsummer to let the plant rebuild energy reserves for next year.

planting.note: Set crowns in early spring in deeply worked, humus-rich soil, positioning the bud at or just below the surface.

directions: Holstein Bloodred is a German heirloom originating in the Holstein region, grown for stalks that run a deep, almost uniform red from base to tip, among the darkest-colored of the traditional European rhubarb strains. It is a heavy-feeding, vigorous grower that rewards an annual topdressing of compost or well-rotted manure with larger, more numerous stalks each following spring. The intense color makes it a favorite for preserves and rhubarb wine, both traditional uses in its region of origin, in addition to the usual pies and sauces. Keep the crown well mulched over winter in colder zones and divide every four to five years to maintain vigor as the clump matures.

planting.note: Plant a dormant crown division in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, setting the bud just below the surface and firming in well.

directions: Grandad's Favourite is a traditional English heirloom passed down through generations of allotment growers and prized for its reliably sweet flavor and tender texture even in stalks left to grow a bit larger than usual. It forces well for an early, pale pink forced crop when covered with a forcing pot in late winter, then produces a second flush of deep red, more strongly flavored stalks in open growth through spring. Established clumps are notably vigorous and long-lived, often remaining productive in the same spot for well over a decade with minimal care beyond an annual mulch. As with other rhubarb, discard the leaves and harvest only the stalks, pulling rather than cutting them from the crown.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F, or start seed indoors in biodegradable pots 3-4 weeks ahead in short-season climates to gain extra time before frost.

directions: Prelude II is a hybrid okra bred to set pods reliably in shorter, cooler growing seasons where classic Southern heirloom okra often struggles to mature a full crop before fall's first frost. Its compact, earlier-flowering plants begin producing spineless green pods notably sooner than tall heirloom types, making it a practical option for northern gardens and short-summer regions that still want a real okra harvest. Soak seed overnight before sowing to speed germination in cool spring soil, and harvest pods every one to two days at two to three inches for the most tender texture. Because the plant stays shorter and more compact than traditional Southern varieties, it tolerates closer spacing and needs less staking in exposed sites.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
